It explains 24 On November 13, 2019, the CEC issued an Order Instituting Rulemaking to begin considering amendments to the Load Management Standards (California Code of Regulations, Title 20, §§ 1621- 1625). The goal was to amend the existing load management standards to increase flexible demand resources through electricity rates, storage, automation, and other measures (Public Resources Code § 25403.5). 73 that the purpose of the 2022 LMS is to “enable a statewide transition from an incentive-based utility command-and-control paradigm to a customer-driven price and GHG signal response paradigm.” It does this by applying four primary requirements to the State’s IOUs, large POUs, and any CCA that provides more than “700 GWh of electricity to customers in any calendar year.” These requirements are: (1) maintain the accuracy of existing and future time-varying rates in MIDAS; (2) “develop a standard rate information access tool to support third-party services”; (3) “develop and submit locational rates that change at least hourly to reflect marginal wholesale costs”; and (4) “integrate information about new time-varying rates and automation technologies into existing customer education and outreach programs” (Herter and Situ 2021). In addition to MIDAS and the 2022 LMS, Herter and Situ (2021) explained that the CEC has undertaken several other relevant actions, two of which are incorporated into Table A1 under the CEC and one under the State Energy Code. First, in response to SB49, in October 2020 the CEC issued an Order Instituting Rulemaking “to adopt regulations to establish standards for flexible demand technologies for appliances (Docket 20-FDAS-01)” in coordination with “existing and future Building Energy Efficiency Standards” and the work toward the 2022 LMS. As part of this rulemaking, the Pre-rulemaking Draft of the Proposed Language for Flexible Demand Appliance Standards, submitted September 30, 2021, first called out the following “types of new appliances sold or offered for sale, rented, leased, or introduced into commerce in California” as subject to the scope of FDAS: (1) electric clothes dryers (both compact and standard); (2) dishwashers (both compact and standard); (3) pool pump controls; and (4) thermostats, specifically low-voltage system thermostats. By February 2024, the final regulatory language was approved for the first FDAS, on pool pump controls. In Fall, 2024, the CEC issued requests for information for low-voltage thermostats and electric vehicle supply equipment. Second, the CEC “provides funding to public and private entities for the advancement of energy research and technology demonstration,” as generated by California’s Electric Program Investment Charge (EPIC), and some of that research and development (R&D) funding has gone toward dynamic pricing and load flexibility (Herter and Situ 2021).
